newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba-economy firmer,but structural problems remain.
newsitem.headline: Buba-economy firmer,but structural problems remain.

text.p: The Bundesbank sounded a cautious note on Germany's economic outlook on Thursday, saying it was unclear whether the economy had overcome its weakness despite a return to buoyant growth in the second quarter.

The Bundesbank said that the economic situation appeared to be improving in several important sectors and, echoing government officials, predicted full-year GDP growth could slightly exceed an earlier government forecast of 0.75 percent.

But a 1.5 percent rise in real second-quarter gross domestic product (GDP) from the first three months overstated the upturn because it was partly fuelled by a resurgence in construction activity after the end of a long, cold winter.
Structural problems also persisted in the economy, the Bundesbank said, adding "they will at best be covered over if the economic upturn continues".

The rise in building activity accounted for about a third of the GDP growth, the bank said in its September monthly report. The economy had shrunk by 0.5 percent in the first quarter as bad weather brought building to a standstill.
"Whether this means the economic weakness which started in the second half of 1995 has already been finally overcome remains to be seen," the Bundesbank said.
"The strong rise in GDP versus the first quarter overstates the impetus behind the economic revival."

While surveys by the Ifo institute showed that sentiment remained poor in many manufacturing companies, the business climate had brightened a little in July, which might indicate the start of a turnaround in sentiment, the report said.
Nevertheless, foreign investment in Germany remained relatively low, indicating urgent action was needed to make the country a more attractive place to do business, it added.

GDP growth was being driven mainly by an increase in foreign demand since the start of the year as economic growth in other industrialised countries fuelled demand for industrial goods, the Bundesbank said.
Heavy rationalisation and moderate pay rises this year had enabled German industry to seize resulting market opportunity.
This year's reversal of the mark's strong appreciation in 1995 had also helped companies by making their goods cheaper in foreign markets, the Bundesbank said.
Meanwhile consumer demand was also beginning to strengthen, probably in a delayed reaction to tax cuts at the start of the year, the Bundesbank said.

"On the other hand, there are certain limits to the further expansion of consumer demand because many consumers are likely to err on the side of caution with regard to spending in view of unemployment risks."
